title: Social and Economic Rights
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the second generation of human rights -- education, health, work, a decent life -- and the long debate over whether they are "real" rights at all.
competenceGoals: explain key social and economic rights and their importance for human dignity
discuss the debate over whether economic and social rights are "real" human rights
analyze the relationship between poverty, inequality, and human rights violations

content.content:
## Can you be free if you are starving?

Here is a question that cuts to the heart of what rights really mean. You may have the legal right to free speech -- but can you exercise it if you never learned to read? You may have the right to vote -- but does it mean much if you are too sick, too hungry or too desperate to take part in society? These questions point to a second category of human rights, sometimes called "second generation" rights: **social and economic rights**.

Where civil and political rights protect you *from* state interference, social and economic rights ask the state to take *positive action* -- to ensure everyone can actually access the basic necessities of life. They are enshrined in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, ratified by more than 170 states. These rights have always been more contested than civil and political ones. During the Cold War, Western nations tended to champion political freedoms while the Soviet bloc emphasised economic rights, and the disagreement became part of the ideological battle. Today, the international consensus is that all human rights are *indivisible and interdependent* -- you cannot fully enjoy one category without the others.

## The right to learn, to work, to live decently

The ICESCR sets out a cluster of concrete rights. The **right to work** (Articles 6 and 7) covers freely chosen employment, just and favourable conditions, fair wages sufficient for a decent living, safe workplaces, and rest and reasonable hours. The **right to social security** (Article 9) protects people against unemployment, sickness, old age and disability. The **right to an adequate standard of living** (Article 11) covers adequate food, clothing and housing, the continuous improvement of living conditions, and freedom from hunger as a fundamental right. The **right to health** (Article 12) means the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health, with access to medical services and disease prevention. And the **right to education** (Articles 13 and 14) guarantees free and compulsory primary education, accessible secondary and higher education, and education aimed at the full development of the human personality.

There is an important catch in how these rights work. States are not expected to deliver everything overnight; instead they are obligated to work toward the **progressive realisation** of these rights, using the maximum of their available resources. Education has a special status here -- it is sometimes called a "multiplier right" because being educated unlocks the ability to enjoy almost every other right. The courage it can take to claim that right is captured by the story of Malala Yousafzai, the Pakistani schoolgirl shot for insisting that girls have the right to learn, who survived and became a global advocate and Nobel laureate. Her case shows that for millions, these are not abstractions but matters of survival and dignity.

questions.task: How do social and economic rights differ from civil and political rights?

options.text: They require the state only to leave people alone

questions.solution: Social and economic rights require positive state action to ensure access to things like education, health and housing, whereas civil and political rights mainly require the state to refrain from interfering.

Rights must be delivered fully and instantly
Rights only apply to progressive governments
Rights get weaker over time

Because it enables the enjoyment of almost all other rights
Because it is the only right that matters

The ICESCR
The English Bill of Rights

questions.solution: Social and economic rights are protected primarily by the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR).

content.content:
## Are they "real" rights? A fair look at both sides

Not everyone agrees that social and economic rights deserve the same status as civil and political ones, and this has been one of the most heated debates in the whole field. It is worth laying out both sides fairly. **For** treating them as full human rights: the UDHR itself makes no distinction between categories of rights; you cannot truly exercise political freedoms without basic material security; the principle of *indivisibility* says all rights are interconnected, so a democracy without social welfare is hollow; and the Vienna Declaration of 1993 explicitly affirmed that all rights are "universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated."

**Against** giving them equal status, or at least urging caution: civil and political rights mostly require the state to *refrain* from acting, whereas economic rights require it to *spend money*; courts find it harder to enforce positive obligations like building hospitals than negative ones like stopping torture, a problem called *justiciability*; some see economic rights as aspirational goals rather than enforceable entitlements; and countries have vastly different resources, making universal standards difficult. The modern consensus leans toward treating all rights as equally important, while taking the practical objections seriously. A key idea bridging the two sides is *minimum core obligations* -- the principle that every state, however poor, must guarantee at least a basic minimum of each right: basic primary education, essential medicines, a minimum of food. Courts in some countries, notably South Africa, have shown that social and economic rights can be meaningfully enforced after all. The deepest barrier, in the end, is not philosophy but poverty and inequality, which remain the greatest obstacles to realising these rights worldwide.

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Which is an argument FOR treating economic and social rights as full human rights?

options.text: They cost nothing to provide
Courts find them very easy to enforce
They apply only to rich countries
The UDHR makes no distinction between categories of rights

questions.solution: Supporters note the UDHR draws no distinction between categories, and that the indivisibility principle ties all rights together.

questions.task: What is the concept of "minimum core obligations"?

options.text: That every state must guarantee at least a basic minimum of each right
That states may ignore poor citizens
That only wealthy states have obligations
That rights apply only in emergencies

questions.solution: Minimum core obligations hold that every state, regardless of resources, must ensure at least a basic minimum of each right -- such as basic education, essential medicines and minimal food.

questions.task: Which document affirmed that all rights are "universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated"?

options.text: The English Bill of Rights (1689)
The Vienna Declaration (1993)
The Treaty of Versailles
The Montreal Protocol

questions.solution: The Vienna Declaration of 1993 affirmed that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated.

questions.task: What does the chapter identify as the greatest barrier to realising these rights worldwide?

options.text: Too many treaties
Excessive education
Poverty and inequality
The Cold War, which is ongoing

questions.solution: The chapter concludes that poverty and inequality remain the greatest barriers to realising social and economic rights worldwide.

content.content:
## In short

Social and economic rights -- the "second generation" -- require states to take positive action so that everyone can access education, health, work, housing and social security, and they are protected by the ICESCR through the principle of progressive realisation. Education is a multiplier right that unlocks all the others. Whether these count as "real" human rights has long been debated: supporters point to the UDHR's refusal to rank rights and to their indivisibility, while sceptics note that they cost money and are harder for courts to enforce. The modern consensus, captured in the 1993 Vienna Declaration, treats all rights as equally important, with minimum core obligations setting a non-negotiable floor. In practice, poverty and inequality remain the biggest obstacles to turning these rights into reality.
